title: Syllabus
content:
Introduction to Second Language Acquisition (Postgraduate) # Note: This syllabus outlines the plan for a 12-week, seminar-style course. Minor adjustments may be made as we progress.
Course Description # This graduate seminar is a research-oriented introduction to how adults acquire second and additional languages. We emphasize linguistic architecture, cross-linguistic variation, interfaces, processing, and implications for teaching, using Slabakova (2016) as the anchor text. Part I establishes language architecture and variation; Part II situates L2 within broader acquisition contexts and highlights the role of input; Part III surveys adult L2 morphology, syntax, the mental lexicon, interfaces, processing, and classroom implications.
Learning Objectives # By the end of the course, students will be able to:
Explain major theoretical proposals in L2 acquisition and how they derive predictions. Critically evaluate empirical studies (design, measures, analyses, interpretations). Compare acquisition across modules (morphology, syntax, lexicon) and interfaces. Relate L2 processing findings (e.g., eye-tracking, ERP) to competence and instruction. Formulate testable research questions and design a feasible study. Articulate pedagogical implications (e.g., Bottleneck Hypothesis; focus on form). Methods of Instruction # Seminar discussions, student-led paper talks, mini-methods workshops, and hands-on data critique. Expect close reading, replication thinking, and constructive debate.
Instructional Materials # Required Text # Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Oxford University Press.
(Designed for advanced undergraduates/graduate students with prior linguistics; emphasizes generative SLA and empirical methods.) Recommended (background / triangulation) # Saville-Troike, M. (2015). Introducing Second Language Acquisition (3rd ed.). Cambridge University Press. Selected journal articles (posted weekly). Assessment & Grading # Participation & Professionalism (10%) — consistent, informed contributions; discussants come prepared. Methods/Analysis Task (20%) — short report critiquing or analyzing data . Reading Journal(20%) — reading summaries (theory, design, findings, alternatives). Final Research Proposal (50%) — 8–10 pages: motivation, literature, hypotheses, design, predicted outcomes. Total = 100%
12-Week Schedule (Topics • Chapters • Key Issues) # We read selectively and thematically; not every section of each chapter is assigned. Page-level reading lists will be posted weekly.
Note: We will not cover Ch. 6 or Ch. 13. Topics are calibrated for first-year MA students with no prior SLA background.
Week 1 — Language Architecture & SLA as a Science # Chapter: Slabakova Ch. 1
Topics: What counts as “knowledge of language”? Core modules (phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics); interfaces; what makes SLA scientific (theory → prediction → test).
Key issues: Evidence in SLA; competence vs. performance; why interfaces can be hard.
Week 2 — Cross-Linguistic Variation & the Learning Task # Chapter: Ch. 2
Topics: What varies across languages; features/parameters in plain language; why variation matters for L2 learning.
Key issues: Initial state and transfer (intuitive examples); falsifiable predictions without heavy formalisms.
Week 3 — Psychological Reality: Using Language in Real Time # Chapter: Ch. 3
Topics: What “processing” means; how the parser uses memory and cues; ambiguity resolution with simple examples.
Key issues: Distinguishing knowledge vs. processing; gentle intro to common tasks (e.g., acceptability judgments).
Week 4 — Age, Input & the Critical Period # Chapter: Ch. 4
Topics: Age effects (pronunciation vs. grammar/meaning); what “critical period” claims mean; role of input amount/quality.
Key issues: Measuring outcomes simply; clear expectations for different subsystems.
Week 5 — Two First Languages (2L1): What It Teaches Us # Chapter: Ch. 5
Topics: Growing up with two languages; how 2L1 patterns inform L2 learning; similarities/differences with adult L2.
Key issues: Transferable insights for L2 classrooms without formal theory overhead.
Week 6 — Locus of Difficulty I: Functional Morphology # Chapter: Ch. 7
Topics: Inflectional morphology (tense, agreement) as a common bottleneck; classic findings explained simply (e.g., missing surface inflection, feature reassembly).
Key issues: Representation vs. performance explanations in plain terms; pedagogical implications.
Week 7 — Locus of Difficulty II: Syntax (the Basics) # Chapter: Ch. 8
Topics: Word order basics; movement in everyday terms; how learners “reset” patterns from L1 to L2.
Key issues: What would count as evidence for/against full acquisition of a structure (no heavy formalism).
Week 8 — The Mental Lexicon # Chapter: Ch. 9
Topics: How words are stored/linked; bilingual lexicon basics; false friends; argument-structure differences via clear examples.
Key issues: Learning and “unlearning” mappings; why some words are harder than others.
Week 9 — Syntax–Semantics Interface (Meaning that Depends on Structure) # Chapter: Ch. 10
Topics: Tense/aspect and other meaning contrasts that hinge on structure; common cross-linguistic mismatches students feel.
Key issues: Why interfaces can be tricky; simple diagnostics to notice interface delays.
Week 10 — Syntax–Discourse & Semantics–Pragmatics Interfaces # Chapter: Ch. 11
Topics: Topic/focus, pronouns, information structure; scalar implicatures and polite meaning beyond the literal.
Key issues: Mapping discourse/pragmatics to form in L2; approachable classroom tasks to probe these mappings.
Week 11 — L2 Processing & Gentle Methods Literacy # Chapter: Ch. 12
Topics: What common tasks look like (GJT, simple reading tasks); how to frame a tiny classroom diagnostic; basics of reliable evidence (controls, sample size at a glance).
Key issues: Linking competence claims to processing predictions—without statistics overload.
Week 12 — Integration, Applications & Proposal Workshop (No new chapter) # Chapters: Review across Chs. 1–5, 7–12 (no Ch. 6, no Ch. 13)
Topics: Pulling it together: language architecture → variation → processing → interfaces → morphology/syntax/lexicon; translating insights to practical, defensible teaching choices.
Key issues: Mini research-proposal pitch (2–3 slides): phenomenon, prediction, a small test (classroom diagnostic acceptable).
Weekly Workflow (Typical) # Before class: Read assigned chapters In class: mini-lectures; student-led seminar; methods/data critique; discussion; synthesis. After class: Update proposal or methods task with new insights. Policies (Highlights) # Attendance & participation are essential to seminar learning. Academic integrity applies to all submissions (cite properly; no AI-generated text without disclosure and permission). Style: APA or LSA; be consistent.

title: Week 1
content:
Week 1 — Language Architecture & SLA as a Science # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 1: Language architecture. Link to Chapter 1
⭐ Overview # What it means to “know a language” and how that knowledge is organized into parts that work together. How SLA uses the scientific method (observe → generalize → hypothesize → test → revise) to make falsifiable predictions. Why theory-to-evidence links matter (e.g., richer agreement systems may correlate with null subjects) and how this connects to teaching relevance. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of Week 1 you should be able to:
Describe, in your own words, what “knowledge of language” is. Name the main parts (sound, word pieces, structure, meaning, use) and say what each does. Explain the basic steps of SLA research (observe → hypothesize → test → revise) and why predictions matter. Give one simple learning/teaching implication that follows from these ideas. 📖 Reading (do before class) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Chapter 1 (focus on the big picture of §§1.1–1.4). Guiding questions while you read
What would count as evidence for/against a claim about L2 knowledge? Where in the architecture would you locate difficulties with agreement vs. word order? 🧠 Key terms # knowledge of language; competence vs. performance; lexicon; phonology; morphology; syntax; semantics; pragmatics; interface; hypothesis; prediction; falsifiability; transfer; null subject
🧩 Core content # 1) What does it mean to “know a language”? # We each carry an internal system that lets us understand and create new sentences. Competence = what you know; Performance = how it comes out in real life (with slips/hesitations). Try it: Think of a sentence you’ve never heard before but still understand—proof your mind can build new meanings from pieces. 2) The building blocks (“modules”) # Phonology: how a language uses sounds (mental categories/patterns). Morphology: meaningful pieces inside words (walk-ed, cat-s). Syntax: how words combine and move (word order, questions, negatives). Semantics: literal, compositional meaning. Pragmatics: meaning from context (implicature, politeness, what’s implied). Try it: Take any short sentence. Label what is sound-related, word-piece related, structure-related, literal meaning, and context-based. 3) Interfaces: when parts meet # Real communication requires coordination between parts (e.g., structure + meaning). Some cross-language differences live at these interfaces, which can feel tricky in an L2. Mini example: English red car vs. a language where the adjective follows the noun. Differences like this can ripple through usage and comprehension. 4) SLA as a science (gentle view) # Steps: observe → suggest an explanation → make a prediction → check whether the prediction holds → adjust if needed. Why “falsifiable”? Explanations should be clear enough that evidence could show them wrong if they’re wrong. Simple illustration (from Chapter 1 themes): If a learner’s L1 often leaves subjects unspoken (null subjects), we might predict more subject omission in their early L2 English—something we can check in beginner data. 5) Why this matters for learning/teaching # Different parts can be hard for different reasons (sound patterns vs. small endings vs. word order vs. meaning-in-context). Knowing the parts helps you notice patterns, set goals, and choose strategies (e.g., targeted listening for sound contrasts; focused reading for small endings; chunking for word order). ✅ Tasks # Before class (preview) # Read Chapter 1 for the big picture; don’t worry about technical detail. Skim “Teaching relevance” notes. Jot down one L2 feature that puzzles you (e.g., articles, agreement, word order, polite meaning). During class (light activities) # Spot-the-part: Label 3–4 sentences for sound, word pieces, structure, literal meaning, and context. Prediction postcard: Write: “If X is true in L1, then beginners might Y in L2.” Keep it concrete and short (one sentence). Practice (micro-lab you can try) # Prompt (approachable): “If L1 allows null subjects but L2 does not, beginners may omit subjects in early L2 English.”
Prediction: beginners from a null-subject L1 omit subjects more often than those from a non-null-subject L1. Simple check: look at a handful of beginner sentences (text or short speech) and note presence/absence of subjects. What would falsify it? No difference across L1 groups, or consistent subjects even at the start. After class (review) # Short reflection:
One idea from Ch. 1, in your own words. One prediction it suggests for L2 learners. One easy way to check that prediction (e.g., a tiny noticing task in readings this week). Self-check:
(1) Define falsifiability and explain why it matters in SLA.
(2) Give one predicted correlation between morphology and syntax.
(3) Why are “Teaching relevance” boxes included?
(4) List the steps of the scientific method in SLA.
(5) Where in the architecture would you locate difficulty with verb movement vs. agreement endings?
🧭 Preview of Week 2 # Next we look at language variation (how languages differ) and why that shapes the SLA learning task—including which features may transfer from L1 and which need new learning.

title: Week 2
content:
Week 2 — Language Variation & the Learning Task" # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 2: Language variation.
Link to Chapter 2
⭐ Overview # How languages differ and what that means for learning a second language. Where variation “lives” in the grammar today (hint: features in the functional lexicon) and why that matters for learners. How prior knowledge from the L1 transfers into the L2 starting point, and what “resetting” involves. Why some areas (e.g., functional morphology and mismatched feature cues) tend to be harder. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of Week 2 you should be able to:
Explain (in plain language) where many cross-language differences come from. Describe the idea of L1 transfer as the initial state and what it predicts. Give one concrete example of how a feature mapping/mismatch can make learning harder. Sketch a simple “if…then” prediction for learner behavior based on a parametric difference. 📖 Reading (do before class) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Chapter 2 (focus on §§2.1–2.4 big picture). As you skim: note any places where the book connects variation → specific learning tasks. Guiding questions while you read
Where does the chapter locate most variation today (lexicon? interfaces?) and why? If your L1 and L2 differ on some feature (e.g., subject expression, word order), what prediction would that make for early L2? 🧠 Key terms # principles & parameters; Minimalist Program; functional lexicon; grammatical features; PF/LF interfaces; transfer; parameter “resetting”; feature exponents; clustering; compounding parameter; learning task
🧩 Core content (gentle, big-picture) # 1) From “big switches” to features in the functional lexicon # Early accounts treated parameters like global on/off switches (e.g., a single “Null Subject” setting predicting a whole cluster of properties). That idea was useful but often too coarse for the cross-linguistic facts. A modern, learner-friendly view: many differences live in the features of functional items (determiners, tense/aspect heads, complementizers, etc.). Learning an L2 means learning which features exist and how they are expressed in that language. Friendly example: Word order differences (e.g., adjective position) often follow from features on functional heads (e.g., N vs. A movement triggers). What felt like a “big switch” is better seen as a few specific feature settings. Try it: Take a simple contrast you know (e.g., subject pronoun use, adjective position). Note the functional word(s) involved and guess which feature might be different (e.g., [+definite], [+topic], [+EPP]). 2) What are “features” (in plain words)? # Think of features as tags of grammatical information attached to functional elements: number, gender, definiteness, person, tense, aspect, case, etc. Crucial point: Languages share meanings but differ in how they signal them (which feature bundles, where they appear, and whether they must be overt). Mini mapping examples: Definiteness: English uses the article the; some languages rely more on word order or context instead of an article. Tense/Aspect: English often marks tense on the verb; other languages distribute aspect across particles or verb classes. Number/Classifiers: English plurals (cats); classifier languages may omit plural marking with numerals and use a classifier instead. Try it: Pick one L2 morpheme you find tricky (e.g., articles). Ask: Which feature(s) is this morpheme carrying here? Is the same meaning split across multiple forms in my L2? 3) Feature exponents and cue reliability # One feature can have many forms (one-to-many), and one form can realize several features (many-to-one). This can make cues less reliable for learners. Examples of cue complexity: English -s can be plural (cats) or 3sg agreement (runs)—same form, different features. Aspect in some languages maps to periphrastic forms (auxiliaries + participles) rather than a single suffix. What this means for learners: When cues are distributed or ambiguous, learners need extra practice to stabilize form–meaning mappings. Quick diagnostic: Given 6 L2 sentences with the same meaning, highlight the different forms used; which mapping is most/least consistent? 4) L1 transfer as the starting point # A practical default: your L1’s feature settings are your initial L2 settings. Early L2 behavior reflects positive transfer (helpful similarities) and negative transfer (overusing an L1 option that the L2 restricts). Friendly predictions: Null subjects: If L1 licenses silent subjects, beginner L2 English may show more dropped subjects. Articles/definiteness: If L1 lacks articles, L2 English learners may over/underuse a/the until feature mappings settle. Word order: If L1 allows more flexible order, learners may initially misplace adverbs/topics in L2. Try it: Write one if-then statement from your L1/L2 pair: “If L1 has X, then early L2 may show Y.” 5) Where learning gets tough (and why) # Functional morphology: Small endings or particles often carry multiple features and interact with syntax/semantics, making them a common bottleneck. Feature reassembly: Learners may have the right meanings but must re-package them using L2-specific forms (e.g., English articles vs. bare nouns with classifiers). Interface load: When meanings depend on structure + context (syntax–semantics, syntax–pragmatics), learners must coordinate multiple systems under time pressure. Processing cost: Less frequent or less reliable cues require more attention and working memory, slowing stabilization. 6) Friendly examples you can visualize # Null subjects: Some languages allow pronoun drop in certain contexts; English typically doesn’t → early omission is predictable for some learners. Articles/definiteness: English demands a/the where other languages use context—expect over/underuse patterns before stabilization. Gender agreement: If L1 lacks grammatical gender, L2 gender marking may show late stabilization (especially with low-salience endings). Tense/Aspect: Learners may conflate habitual vs. completed events if L1/L2 carve up aspect differently. Compounding & resultatives: Some languages productively allow N+N compounds and resultative constructions; others restrict them—useful for order-of-difficulty predictions. 7) Simple diagnostics (low-stress, class-ready) # Minimal pair sort: Give pairs differing by a single feature (e.g., the cat vs. a cat). Ask learners to sort by meaning/use; discuss the feature behind the contrast. Cloze with choices: Provide short texts where a feature is realized in different ways (articles, aspect). Have learners choose the most natural option and justify the feature logic. Judgment strip: 8–10 short sentences targeting one feature (some well-formed, some not). Quick acceptable/unacceptable ticks → look for pattern, not perfection. Production nudge: Prompts eliciting the target feature (e.g., describing pictures to force reference tracking or aspect choices). 8) What success looks like (for Week 2) # You can name a cross-language difference and locate it as a feature mapping (not just “grammar is different”). You can write a clear if-then prediction from that difference. You can propose a tiny check (sorting, cloze, judgments, or a short production prompt) that would confirm or challenge your prediction. ✅ Tasks # Before class (preview) # Read Ch. 2 for the main ideas (don’t get lost in technical terms). Bring one L1 ↔ L2 difference you’ve noticed (word order? subject expression? compounding?). We’ll use it to make a prediction. In class (light activities) # Feature hunt (pairs, 8–10 min): Pick one L1↔L2 contrast and say which feature(s) might be different and how they surface. If-then postcards (small groups, 10 min): Write one sentence: “If L1 has X, then beginners may Y in L2.” Keep it observable (Y should be something you can count or notice). Practice (micro-lab you can try) # Prompt (approachable): “If a learner’s L1 freely drops subjects but the L2 does not, early L2 subject omission should be higher for that learner group.”
Design idea: Compare a few beginner sentences (two L1 groups). Count subject present/absent. What would falsify it? No group difference; or consistent subjects from the start.
(This mirrors how Chapter 2 turns theory into learning tasks and predictions.) After class (review) # Mini reflection (≈150–200 words):
Name one L1↔L2 difference in features or feature exponents. Write an if-then prediction it suggests. One easy way you could check it (e.g., quick corpus search; classroom samples). Self-check (answers hidden):
(1) Where does the Minimalist view largely locate variation?
(2) Why can feature–form mismatches be hard for L2 learners?
(3) What does L1 transfer predict about the initial L2 grammar?
(4) State one area often predicted to be harder than narrow syntax.
📖 Additional resources (short articles/chapters) # White, L. (1985). The “pro-drop” parameter in adult second language acquisition. Language Learning, 35(1), 47–61. Snyder, W. (2001). On the nature of syntactic variation: Evidence from complex predicates and complex word-formation. Language, 77(2), 324–342. Biberauer, T. (2008). Introducing parameters. In The Bantu-Romance Connection. 🧭 Preview of Week 3 # We shift from what varies to how language is processed: what the parser does online and how processing interacts with grammatical knowledge.

title: Week 3
content:
Week 3 — Processing & the Parser: How L2 is Used in Real Time # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 3: The psychological reality of language in use. Link to Chapter 3
⭐ Overview # What “processing” means: how the mind builds meaning in real time during listening/reading and plans forms during speaking. Big ideas: the parser, timing, limited resources, and why learners sometimes rely on easier cues (semantics/discourse) over costly structure when time is tight. What common methods actually measure (self-paced reading, eye-tracking, ERP) and how to read their basic signals. Why this matters: classroom input and tasks can shape processing (e.g., highlighting small forms, pacing, repeated exposure). 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of Week 3 you should be able to:
Explain, in plain terms, what the parser does and why time/attention matter. Recognize what self-paced reading, eye-tracking, and ERPs can tell us about L2 processing. State one simple prediction about when L2 learners might rely more on meaning cues than syntax (and why). Suggest one teaching move that eases processing demands for a difficult form. 📖 Reading (do before class) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Chapter 3 (read for big picture; you don’t need technical detail). As you skim, note: which findings suggest time pressure or memory limits shape L2 behavior? Guiding questions while you read
What’s the difference between “having a rule” and using it quickly while reading/listening? Which cues (lexical meaning, word order, agreement endings, discourse context) feel fast/easy vs. slow/costly? 🧠 Key terms # parser; incremental processing; garden-path; Good-Enough comprehension; cue-based retrieval; working memory; surprisal/predictability; self-paced reading (SPR); eye-tracking; regressions; ERP (N400, P600); ambiguity resolution; speed–accuracy trade-off
🧩 Core content (gentle, big-picture) # 1) What “processing” is (and isn’t) # Competence is stored knowledge; processing is the on-the-fly construction of structure/meaning with limited time and attention. The parser builds interpretations incrementally—word by word—sometimes making early guesses that must be revised. Try it: Read quickly: While the man hunted the deer ran into the woods.
Did you initially attach the deer as the object of hunted? That’s a garden-path—your parser made a fast guess, then had to rebuild.
2) Common processing architectures (friendly snapshot) # Serial/modular flavor: syntax builds first, semantics/pragmatics integrate a beat later. Interactive/constraint-based flavor: multiple cues (lexical, frequency, discourse) compete at once. Good-Enough idea: under load, the system may settle for a plausible parse, not a perfect one. Why this matters for L2: If resources are tight, learners may lean more on meaning/plausibility and less on fine-grained structure—especially at lower proficiency or in noisy input.
3) Methods you will see in papers (what the signals mean) # Self-Paced Reading (SPR): word-by-word times. Longer times = more processing cost (e.g., at a disambiguating region). Eye-tracking: where eyes land, first-pass times, and regressions (looking back) show difficulty and reanalysis. ERP (EEG): N400 (≈ semantic fit, lexical access)—larger when a word is less expected/meaning-incongruent. P600 (≈ structural reanalysis/violation)—larger when structure clashes or must be repaired. You don’t need formulas—just the intuition: bigger signal or slower time = harder at that moment.
4) What tends to happen in L2 (and why) # Timing: lexical access and integration can be slower, leaving less time for complex structure before the next word arrives. Cue weighting: learners may over-rely on semantics/discourse (highly helpful) and under-use subtle morphosyntax (costly, low-salience). Proficiency & exposure: with practice and input, structural cues become faster, and reliance re-balances. Task demands: time pressure pushes Good-Enough outcomes; relaxed tasks allow full structure use. Friendly prediction: If a structure is late-learned and low-salience (e.g., agreement endings), learners will rely more on word order or plausibility in fast reading.
5) Small forms, big load # Functional morphology (agreement, tense/aspect marking) can carry a lot of grammatical work in tiny pieces; it is perceptually low-salience and easy to miss online. Interfaces (syntax↔semantics, syntax↔pragmatics) require coordinating multiple systems under time pressure → higher risk of slowdowns or Good-Enough interpretations. 6) Classroom implications (processing-aware teaching) # Enhance salience of small forms (bold/underline in reading cycles; brief auditory emphasis). Control pace (shorter sentences first; chunking; guided pauses) to allow structure to “catch up.” Repeat exposure to the same form–meaning mapping across varied but simple contexts. Minimal pair noticing (e.g., He run vs. He runs) with quick meaning checks to tie form → interpretation. ✅ Tasks # Before class (preview) # Read Chapter 3 for the big picture (don’t worry about technical terms). Jot down one sentence that misled you at first read (a mini garden-path or tricky agreement). In class (light activities) # Garden-path live: Three short ambiguous sentences; mark where your interpretation flips. Share which cue (syntax/meaning/punctuation) fixed it. Signal decoder: Given a simple plot (fake data) of SPR or eye-tracking, say where the difficulty happened and why (one sentence). Practice (micro-lab you can try) # Prompt: “When time is tight, learners rely more on meaning/plausibility than fine structure.”
Design idea: Create 6 short items where syntax conflicts with a plausible reading (e.g., agreement or filler–gap). Check: In a quick yes/no acceptability or timed choice, do learners prefer the plausible option over the strictly grammatical one? Falsifier: No plausibility bias (or a stronger structure bias) even under time pressure. After class (review) # Mini reflection (≈150–200 words):
Describe a case where you caught yourself using Good-Enough comprehension. Say which cue you favored (meaning? word order? morphology?) and why. One idea to train the less-used cue next week. Self-check (answers hidden):
(1) Why do garden-path sentences cause slowdowns?
(2) Define similarity-based interference in cue-based retrieval.
(3) Give one reason online measures can diverge from offline accuracy in L2.
(4) What pattern would support a processing (not competence) account for an L2 difficulty?
(5) Name one ERP component associated with morpho-syntactic violations and its interpretation.
📖 Additional resources (short articles/chapters) # Clahsen, H., & Felser, C. (2006). Grammatical processing in language learners. Applied Psycholinguistics, 27(1), 3–42. Kaan, E. (2014). Predictive sentence processing in L2 and L1. Linguistic Approaches to Bilingualism, 4(2), 257–282. Cunnings, I. (2017). Interference in native and non-native sentence processing. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition, 20(4), 712–721. Hopp, H. (2010). Ultimate attainment in L2 inflection: Moving beyond age. Second Language Research, 26(1), 129–160. Jegerski, J. (2016). Self-paced reading in SLA research. In The Routledge Handbook of SLA (methods chapter; short and practical). 🧭 Preview of Week 4 # Next we look at age, input, and the critical period debate—how outcomes differ across subsystems (pronunciation vs. morphosyntax/meaning) and how input quality/quantity fits into the picture.

title: Week 4
content:
Week 4 — Age, Input & the Critical Period # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 4: The Critical Period Hypothesis. Link to Chapter 4
⭐ Overview # What the Critical Period Hypothesis (CPH) claims and why age might matter for language learning. How age of acquisition (AoA) interacts with input amount/quality, use, and education. Why age effects differ across subsystems: phonology (accent) vs. morphosyntax/semantics (mixed evidence). What counts as persuasive evidence (tasks, outcomes, controls) and what would falsify a strong CPH claim. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of Week 4 you should be able to:
Explain the basic idea of a critical/sensitive period for L2 and the kinds of evidence used to test it. Distinguish AoA from other predictors (length of residence, input quality, education, use). Describe why phonology typically shows stronger age effects than morphosyntax/semantics. Write one if–then prediction about age and outcomes, and say what result would challenge that prediction. 📖 Reading (do before class) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Chapter 4 (read for big picture). As you read, note: Which results support a sharp cut-off vs. a gradual (sensitive) period? What confounds did studies try to control? Guiding questions while you read
Is there one “critical” period or are there multiple timelines for different subsystems? What would falsify a strong CPH (e.g., late starters reaching native-like levels under strict controls)? 🧠 Key terms # critical period; sensitive period; AoA (age of acquisition); length of residence (LoR); input amount/quality; ultimate attainment; near-native; confound; phonology vs. morphosyntax; aptitude; practice/use; outcome measures
🧩 Core content (gentle, big-picture) # 1) What the CPH says (and softer variants) # Strong (hard) CPH: after a specific age window, native-like attainment is no longer possible. Sensitive-period view: age effects are gradual; later starters can improve a lot, but probability of fully native-like outcomes declines with AoA. Friendly takeaway: Age matters, but how it matters depends on what you measure and how carefully you measure it. 2) What outcomes are we talking about? # Phonology (accent): shows robust age effects—late starters often retain a detectable accent even with long residence. Morphosyntax/semantics: more mixed; late near-natives exist, especially with high-quality input, education, and deliberate practice. Pragmatics/discourse: can be challenging well past childhood due to context-dependent mappings and lower salience. 3) Measuring “ultimate attainment” (why methods matter) # Tasks: global ratings (accent/intelligibility), grammaticality judgments, sentence interpretation, timed processing measures. Baselines: who counts as a “native” control? Are items balanced and independent of vocabulary/background knowledge? Confounds: education, socioeconomic factors, exposure, use, motivation, aptitude—all can inflate or mask age effects. Friendly rule: the stronger the design (clean baselines, good controls, reliable measures), the clearer the age pattern you can interpret. 4) AoA versus input/use (don’t mix them up) # AoA is not the same as time in the L2. Two late starters with the same AoA can diverge if one gets richer input, more use, or formal schooling. Prediction: Under matched input/education, age effects will still appear—especially in phonology—but may be smaller in some morphosyntactic domains. 5) Shapes of the function (what curves look like) # Step-like (hard CPH): sharp drop after a boundary (e.g., puberty). Continuous (sensitive period): gradual decline with no sharp cliff. Hybrid: steep early decline that flattens later—common in real datasets. 6) Why subsystems differ # Phonology depends on early-tuned perceptual categories and fine motor patterns → strong age effects. Morphosyntax/semantics can be explicitly taught, are rehearsable, and benefit from literacy and education → more late success cases. Interfaces (structure + context) add processing load, which can exacerbate age effects when time pressure is high. 7) What would count as evidence—for or against? # Supports CPH: a monotonic AoA effect remains after controlling input/use/education; late starters cluster below native range on demanding measures. Challenges CPH: documented late near-natives meeting strict performance criteria; AoA slope weakens or disappears once confounds are rigorously controlled. Falsifier (hard CPH): many late starters consistently within native distribution on multiple independent measures. ✅ Tasks # Before class (preview) # Read Ch. 4 for the big picture (don’t stress about statistics). Note one result you found persuasive and one you found questionable, and why. In class (light activities) # Curve sketching (pairs, 8–10 min): Draw three possible AoA→attainment curves (step, linear decline, steep-then-flat). Label which subsystem each curve might reflect. Confound detective (small groups, 10 min): Given a short study description, list at least three confounds to control (e.g., LoR, input quality, literacy). Practice (micro-lab you can try) # Prompt: “AoA predicts accent strength more strongly than morphosyntax outcomes.”
Plan: Collect (or imagine) small samples for accent ratings and a morphosyntax judgment score, each paired with AoA. Prediction: AoA correlates more tightly with accent than with morphosyntax. Falsifier: Comparable (or stronger) AoA correlation for morphosyntax after controlling LoR and input. After class (review) # Mini reflection (≈150–200 words):
State one if–then prediction about AoA and an outcome you care about. Name two confounds you would control and one way to measure success. Self-check (answers hidden):
What’s the difference between critical and sensitive period claims? Why is phonology often more age-sensitive than morphosyntax? Give two confounds that can mimic age effects. What would falsify a hard CPH? State one falsifiable prediction of a strong CPH for L2. Give an example where measure choice changes the age conclusion. Define input quality and give a diagnostic example. Name two covariates that must be controlled in AoA studies. What result would favor a sensitive-period over a strict CPH? 📖 Additional resources (short articles/chapters) # Johnson, J. S., & Newport, E. L. (1989). Critical period effects in second language learning. Cognitive Psychology, 21(1), 60–99. Birdsong, D., & Molis, M. (2001). On the evidence for maturational constraints in SLA. Journal of Memory and Language, 44(2), 235–249. DeKeyser, R. M. (2000). The robustness of critical period effects in second language acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 22(4), 499–533. Flege, J. E., Yeni-Komshian, G., & Liu, S. (1999). Age constraints on second-language acquisition. Journal of Memory and Language, 41(1), 78–104. Long, M. H. (1990). Maturational constraints on language development. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 12(3), 251–285. 🧭 Preview of Week 5 # Next we compare acquisition contexts: two first languages (2L1), child L2, multilingual and heritage learners—and what these profiles teach us about mechanisms of L2 development.
